2013.problem: Malicious actors coordinate covertly within live streams, evading detection while appearing normal.
2013.approach: Model rooms as bags and action-timeslot sequences as instances within a Multiple Instance Learning framework capturing behavioral patterns.
2013.contribution: AC-MIL framework outperforms baselines on real Douyin data, offering both risk scores and interpretable behavioral evidence.
2013.bp: Live streaming platforms host millions of rooms with minimal human moderation. Coordinated bad actors (scam groups, harassment mobs) hide inside normal-looking chats but cause real harms. The goal is catching these campaigns before they escalate, without manually reviewing millions of hours of footage.
2013.wh: The core tension: you see only room-level signals ("this room is risky") but the bad actors disperse their actions across users and time windows, camouflaging themselves within normal chatter. You can't label individual user actions cheaply, only say whether a whole room was problematic, making this a weak-supervision nightmare.
2013.ap: The paper treats each live room as a bag of instances, where instances are time-windowed behavioral capsules (what one user did in minutes 5-10, etc.). Instead of assuming bad actions all come from one spot, they build a neural encoder that watches both individual user arcs and cross-user coordination patterns. Multi-scale temporal and graph signals feed into a single room-risk score.
2013.ww: Multiple Instance Learning sidesteps the labeling bottleneck by learning from room labels alone. Capsule sequences let the model discover that *sequences* of actions matter more than isolated events. Modeling both serial (one user over time) and parallel (many users at once) paths lets it spot when disparate actions synchronize—the hallmark of coordination.
2013.po: On Douyin's industrial data, AC-MIL catches malicious rooms with less false alarms than prior MIL/sequential methods. It also points to *why* a room is risky (which user-timeslot sequences triggered the flag), giving moderation teams actionable leads rather than opaque predictions.

2014.problem: LLMs generate educational questions at low cognitive levels, favoring recall over deep thinking.
2014.approach: Evaluate and improve six LLMs via Bloom's Taxonomy through prompt design and measure cognitive shift intensity.
2014.contribution: Refined prompts reduce repetitiveness by 24.45% and boost higher-order cognition by 11.53% on diverse subjects.
2014.bp: Digital tutoring is exploding, and LLMs can draft unlimited problem sets on-demand. But most generated questions just ask "which formula applies?" when deep learning means figuring out *why* that formula works in a new context. Schools need a way to push LLMs to ask the hard questions automatically.
2014.wh: LLMs trained on massive text default to pattern-matching, which tends toward fact retrieval. The prompting strategy must actively steer toward synthesis, evaluation, and creation (top levels of Bloom's). Without explicit guidance, the model prints easier, repetitive questions—they're statistically likelier and require less reasoning.
2014.ap: They analyze 20,700 questions from six LLMs (Qwen, InternLM, Claude, etc.) across CS, K-12 math, social science using Bloom's six levels. A human-AI protocol tags each question's cognitive level. Then they test new prompts that explicitly request multi-level questions and measure *cognitive shift intensity*—how much the model jumps from recall to analysis to creation.
2014.ww: Targeted prompts work because they make the cognitive demand *explicit* in the input, removing the model's freedom to default to easier reasoning. By measuring shift intensity (how much the model moves *between* cognitive levels), they capture whether it's genuinely stretching or just adding complexity. Chain-of-Thought refinement lets the model self-correct during generation.
2014.po: InternLM3-8B's higher-order output jumps from ~60% to 71%, and questions repeat 24% less on Qwen. The paper gives educators/LLM teams reproducible prompts and metrics to audit their generation systems, enabling personalized learning at scale without a tutor.

2015.problem: Efficiently counting four-cycles in massive streaming graphs is hard; prior bounds don't leverage graph sparsity.
2015.approach: Two streaming algorithms using induced subgraph sampling, tailored to degeneracy and cycle distribution.
2015.contribution: Two-pass algorithm achieves optimal bounds for sparse graphs; one-pass works on real sparse/social networks.
2015.bp: Four-cycles (two-hop friendships that return) are a motif of trust, collaboration, or fraud in networks—they signal tight communities. Platforms process graph edges in one shot (stream), can't store the full graph, yet need fast cycle counts for clustering coefficients, anomaly signals, or recommendation scoring.
2015.wh: Counting cycles exactly is Γ(m^{3/2}) or worse; you can't afford that at streaming scale. Existing approximations treat all edges equally, ignoring that real networks are sparse (bounded degeneracy). Also, cycles can cluster on a few nodes (unfair distribution) or spread evenly—a one-size-fits-all algorithm fails both cases.
2015.ap: Algorithm 1 (two-pass): sample induced subgraphs proportional to degeneracy κ and triangle-wedge abundance. Store enough samples to estimate the full count with error bounds ε. Algorithm 2 (one-pass): same idea but keep only one stream buffer; works when cycles don't concentrate on single nodes/edges. Both use classic reservoir sampling to stay in O(κm/√T) space.
2015.ww: Degeneracy κ (max min-degree in any subgraph) is usually much smaller than m for real networks, cutting space by orders of magnitude. Sampling induced subgraphs preserves local structure; counting cycles within them recovers global counts. Cycle distribution awareness lets Algorithm 2 handle the common case (social networks) with one pass, not two.
2015.po: On real social and collaboration graphs, both algorithms beat prior streaming methods on space/accuracy tradeoff. Algorithm 1 matches the known lower bound Ω(m/√T) up to log factors for constant-degeneracy graphs, proving optimality. Practitioners get practical code that works on billion-node networks.

2016.problem: Multi-behavior recommendations ignore latent user preferences and suffer from low-entropy behaviors to high-entropy items asymmetry.
2016.approach: Generative diffusion model from agnostic to behavior-specific latent preferences via multimodal autoencoders and RoPE.
2016.contribution: FatsMB framework learns diverse, accurate recommendations on multi-behavior sequences.
2016.bp: Users interact with platforms in many ways: clicking, sharing, liking, purchasing. Each signal means something different. A click says "I noticed this," a purchase says "I committed money." Mixing them naively loses the nuance. The real win is predicting *which item to recommend next* by synthesizing all signals into a unified preference profile.
2016.wh: Prior models treat behaviors as rigid channels or map them all to the target (purchase) deterministically. But user preferences are latent and fuzzy—the same user preference could lead to a click (low-barrier) or a purchase (commitment). Deterministic scoring can't capture this ambiguity; sparse, skewed behaviors (many clicks, few purchases) make dense discrimination impossible.
2016.ap: They train a Multi-Behavior AutoEncoder (MBAE) that compresses all behaviors into a joint latent preference space. Then a diffusion model generates new preferences in that space, starting from noisy random vectors and refining toward target-behavior specific outputs. Behavior-aware RoPE (rotary positional embeddings) fuses information across behavior channels during this generation process.
2016.ww: Diffusion models excel at capturing uncertainty and diversity because they learn *distributions*, not point estimates. Starting from noise and iteratively refining is gentler than direct scoring, especially on low-entropy behaviors. The MBAE bottleneck forces the model to find a true shared representation, and RoPE fusion ensures behavior-specific signals (e.g., purchase bias) guide the final refinement.
2016.po: FatsMB generates diverse candidate recommendations with proper uncertainty estimates, outperforming prior behavior-fixed and behavior-specific methods. Users get fresh, accurate suggestions tailored to their latent preferences across all interaction types, not just the dominant behavior.

2017.problem: GPU-based vector search suffers low throughput and high P99 latency due to query-centric kernels and inefficient batching.
2017.approach: Cluster-centric GPU kernel and hitch-ride ordering preserve query order while batching computation across queries.
2017.contribution: 22× lower P99 latency and 9× higher throughput via data reuse and smart task reordering.
2017.bp: Vector search powers search engines, recommendation feeds, LLM retrieval, and ranking. The bottleneck: millions of simultaneous queries (users asking "find similar documents") against billion-sized vector databases. GPUs can parallelize, but current designs waste their potential, leaving queries waiting or forcing expensive data moves.
2017.wh: Query-centric kernels process each query independently, loading data into GPU shared memory just for that query, then discarding it. The next query reloads the same data. Batch reordering optimizes throughput but breaks query-arrival order, so slow queries stall fast ones—killing user-facing latency guarantees.
2017.ap: Hitcher reverses the thinking: group queries by *cluster* (which database vectors they search). One GPU block handles many queries against the same data chunk, reusing that chunk in shared memory. Within a batch, hitch-ride ordering runs queries in arrival order but *batches computation* on shared data. CPU and multi-GPU paths offload cold data, reducing PCIe traffic.
2017.ww: Cluster-centric kernels maximize data locality and shared-memory reuse—GPUs excel here. Hitch-ride ordering is the key insight: you don't need queries to *wait* for batch formation if you batch only the *compute* on already-loaded data. Arrival order is preserved for the user; efficiency is preserved for the hardware.
2017.po: Real-world benchmarks show P99 latency drops from 500ms to 20ms (22×) and throughput grows 9×, crucial for LLM systems serving human chat and interactive search. Hitcher is a drop-in optimization for existing vector-search systems.

2018.problem: Text-Rich Networks ignore hierarchical semantics in node documents; flat models miss coarse and fine semantic structure.
2018.approach: Build implicit hierarchical taxonomy via similarity-guided contrastive learning and LLM refinement, then regularize embeddings to align with it.
2018.contribution: TIER learns hierarchical representations for nodes, improving interpretability and downstream task performance.
2018.bp: Knowledge graphs, document networks, and paper citation graphs naturally embody hierarchies: broad topics branch into subtopics, then specific techniques. A flat node embedding loses this structure, treating "deep learning" and "backpropagation" as unrelated nodes. Preserving hierarchy lets systems discover coarse clusters (research areas) and fine-grain distinctions (methods) together.
2018.wh: Hierarchical structure isn't usually explicit in graph data; it's latent in node text and edge semantics. Existing TRN models either ignore text (pure GNNs) or treat it as a flat feature (no hierarchy). Building a hierarchy automatically is hard: you need to cluster docs at multiple levels without ground truth, then enforce that hierarchy doesn't contradict the learned embeddings.
2018.ap: TIER first runs contrastive learning on node texts to create a clustering-friendly embedding space. Then hierarchical K-Means discovers level-by-level clusters, and an LLM refines those clusters (checking coherence, merging/splitting as needed). Finally, cophenetic correlation (a measure of hierarchy-embedding alignment) is added as a regularization loss during embedding training, pulling similar vectors to appropriate hierarchy levels.
2018.ww: Contrastive learning surfaces natural clusters in text because the model learns to push semantically similar nodes together. Hierarchical K-Means respects that structure while discovering levels. LLM refinement catches mistakes that geometric clustering alone would miss. Cophenetic loss is elegant: it penalizes embeddings that contradict the hierarchy, guiding the model to learn representations faithful to both semantics and structure.
2018.po: Learned embeddings now encode hierarchical information, enabling coarse topic grouping and fine-grain distinctions. Downstream tasks (link prediction, node classification) improve, and interpretability jumps because you can ask "why are these nodes related?" at multiple levels.

2019.problem: Traffic forecasting ignores sudden incidents (accidents, weather) that dramatically alter flow patterns unpredictably.
2019.approach: Incident-Guided Spatiotemporal GNN with modules for heterogeneous incident impact and decay dynamics.
2019.contribution: IGSTGNN with incident dataset significantly improves prediction accuracy during anomalous periods.
2019.bp: Traffic departments manage thousands of sensors across city grids, predicting flows 15 minutes ahead to route traffic, signal timing, and ramp metering. Historical patterns work until an accident shuts lanes or a thunderstorm hits—then predictions fail catastrophically because incidents are rare and hard to predict in advance.
2019.wh: Most forecasting models (GNNs, RNNs, Transformers) learn patterns from historical sequences. Incidents are outliers that break patterns. Including them as inputs is tempting but naive: incidents are rare (you can't learn to predict them), and their impact varies wildly (small fender-bender vs. multi-car pileup on a highway vs. minor fender-bender on a surface street).
2019.ap: IGSTGNN splits incident handling into two modules. Incident-Context Spatial Fusion (ICSF) captures *where* an incident hits and its heterogeneous ripple (a highway accident affects distant intersections more than a side-street fender-bender). Temporal Incident Impact Decay (TIID) models *when* the incident fades—congestion doesn't disappear instantly but dissipates over minutes as vehicles clear.
2019.ww: By separating spatial (where) and temporal (when) components, IGSTGNN avoids treating all incidents alike. ICSF learns context-aware diffusion; a major highway accident spreads impact further than a minor surface-street one. TIID learns decay curves; rush hour takes longer to recover than mid-day. The paper also releases a curated incident-timestamped dataset, enabling the model to learn these patterns.
2019.po: On the new benchmark, IGSTGNN predicts flow during incidents far better than prior methods (including ones fed incident labels). Cities get actionable 15-minute predictions even during crises, improving response times and detour routing.

2020.problem: Recommender profiles lack richness; unclear how to construct and propagate them for diverse knowledge sources.
2020.approach: Use LLMs to extract semantic profiles for KG entities, integrate via knowledge graph, match at training.
2020.contribution: SPiKE recommendation model combining LLM profiles with KG propagation consistently beats baselines.
2020.bp: Recommendation systems thrive when they know *why* users care about items. A user interested in machine learning papers, data visualization tools, and research conferences has a coherent profile. Knowledge graphs encode *structural* links ("this paper cites that") but not *semantic* richness ("this paper's core insight is regularization"). LLMs can extract that richness.
2020.wh: Prior KG-based recommenders treat entities as isolated nodes, missing semantic nuance. Profile-based recommenders assume hand-crafted profiles (expensive). LLMs can generate text-based profiles, but profiles alone don't propagate influence through the graph. A single rich profile on one entity stays local; you need the graph to amplify.
2020.ap: SPiKE has three stages. First, LLMs generate semantic profiles for all KG entities ("who is this person, what are they known for"). Second, these profiles are embedded and integrated into the KG, enriching the graph structure. Third, during training, user-item preference matching aligns LLM-based semantic representations with learned KG-based embeddings via contrastive loss.
2020.ww: LLMs excel at reasoning over diverse knowledge sources and compressing into rationale-like profiles. KGs propagate those profiles to neighbors via graph walks, letting entity richness inform far-away users. Contrastive learning during training ensures both modalities (semantic + structural) pull toward the same preference signal, avoiding conflicts.
2020.po: SPiKE beats KG-only and LLM-only recommenders on real datasets. Users get recommendations grounded in both structural similarity ("others like you liked this") and semantic coherence ("this aligns with your inferred interests"). Profiles are also interpretable—you can read why an item was suggested.

2021.problem: Federated GNNs face high communication costs and non-IID data across decentralized clients.
2021.approach: Generative diffusion models on each client capture local graph distributions, shared with server, then generate synthetic graphs.
2021.contribution: CeFGC reduces communication to three rounds via generative models, handling non-IID data and proving constant-round complexity.
2021.bp: Hospitals, banks, and research labs hold sensitive graph data they can't share. Federated learning trains a shared model by keeping data local and sending only parameter updates. But GNNs need the full neighborhood structure to compute gradients; sharing parameters across dozens of rounds with dozens of clients drains bandwidth and battery on edge devices.
2021.wh: Naive federated GNNs send model parameters every round (linear in clients). Non-IID data (one hospital's patient graph differs from another's) causes model drift—each client trains on biased local data. Traditional averaging doesn't account for local graph structure variance.
2021.ap: CeFGC inverts the flow: clients *generate* not *transmit*. Each client trains a local generative diffusion model that captures its graph distribution. This generative model (smaller than the GNN) goes to the server, which redistributes it to all clients. Clients use it to generate synthetic graphs matching the server's aggregate distribution, mix with their local graphs, train local GNNs, and send only the trained weights back—three total rounds.
2021.ww: Generative diffusion models are compact (fewer parameters than a GNN) and statistical (capture distribution, not data). Synthetic-graph augmentation addresses non-IID by giving each client exposure to the aggregate distribution. A single diffusion model round is cheaper than many parameter-exchange rounds. Theoretically, three rounds is provably optimal for this setup.
2021.po: On graph datasets (molecular, citation), CeFGC matches centralized GNN performance with 3-10× communication reduction. Edge devices and privacy-sensitive organizations can train better GNNs without leaking data, enabling federated knowledge discovery.

2022.problem: Cognitive diagnosis models are brittle to noise in learner response data and rely on hand-tuned architecture design.
2022.approach: Evolutionary multi-objective NAS to search architecture space while training a weight-sharing supernet robust to noise.
2022.contribution: OSCD improves cognitive diagnosis robustness via architecture search; validated on intelligent tutoring systems.
2022.primary_theme: Neural architecture search and online learning
2022.bp: Online tutoring platforms know student responses (right/wrong) on knowledge concepts and infer what they've mastered. Accurate diagnosis enables adaptive learning—give harder problems to fast learners, review basics with strugglers. But real student data is noisy (guessing, off-day performance) and tutoring systems need models that ignore noise and generalize to new students.
2022.wh: Standard cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) assume clean labels. Real tutoring data is corrupted: students guess, misclick, or rush. Also, CDM architectures are hand-designed by researchers (rules like "use RNN for temporal, graph for prerequisite structure"), missing better designs that aren't obvious. Manual design limits generalization.
2022.ap: OSCD applies evolutionary NAS to cognitive diagnosis. It constructs a search space of architectural options (temporal modules, graph modules, fusion strategies, attention blocks) and trains a weight-sharing supernet via a complete binary tree topology—each node is a choice point. Then an evolutionary multi-objective optimizer searches for architectures that balance accuracy *and* noise robustness.
2022.ww: Weight-sharing supernets (one model representing many architectures) are efficient; each architectural path reuses weights. Multi-objective search ensures you don't just optimize accuracy (which can overfit to noise) but also robustness (which reduces sensitivity to label errors). Tree topology is elegant for binary branching decisions.
2022.po: OSCD finds architectures that diagnose student mastery accurately even with noisy response labels. On real ITS data, discovered models outperform hand-tuned baselines, and robustness metrics confirm reduced noise sensitivity. Tutoring platforms get adaptive systems that work with messy real data.

2023.problem: Multimodal medical image fusion lacks generalizability, is computationally expensive, and vulnerable to adversarial attacks.
2023.approach: Efficient attention blocks for modality-specific patterns and cross-attention for complementary shared representations; extend with adversarial robustness.
2023.contribution: MAIL and Robust-MAIL networks achieve superior performance on 20 datasets with 42× fewer parameters than state-of-the-art.
2023.bp: A patient with a tumor gets MRI, CT, and SPECT scans—each modality reveals different tissue properties. Fusing them improves diagnosis (tumor boundary, type, staging) beyond any single modality. Clinics need fast, reliable systems that work across disease types and imaging hardware, not bespoke models per modality or disease.
2023.wh: Naive fusion (concatenate features) misses modality-specific structure and wastes computation. Modality-specific models don't share complementary signals—one modality might excel at boundary detection while another excels at tissue density. Existing methods are compute-heavy, locking out resource-limited clinics. Adversarial noise (imperceptible perturbations) can flip diagnosis, a reliability nightmare in medicine.
2023.ap: MAIL combines two components. Efficient residual attention blocks capture modality-specific multi-scale patterns without heavy computation. A cross-attention module learns complementary shared representations (the fusion) by attending across modality channels. Robust-MAIL adds random projection filters and modulated attention noise during training, teaching the model to ignore subtle adversarial perturbations.
2023.ww: Attention mechanisms let the model learn *where* to focus within each modality (boundary vs. density) and *which* modalities to trust for each task. Residual learning keeps computation lean. Random projections + noise augmentation simulate adversarial attacks during training, forcing robustness without expensive adversarial optimization.
2023.po: MAIL matches or beats heavy models on 20 public datasets while using 42× fewer parameters—clinics can deploy on GPUs or even CPUs. Robust-MAIL additionally resists adversarial attacks, critical for safety-critical medical AI. Generalization improves: same model works across multiple diseases and imaging protocols.

2024.problem: Unsupervised multimodal entity alignment suffers imbalanced pseudo-seed coverage, limiting contrastive learning across sparsely-connected entities.
2024.approach: Quality enhancement of pseudo-seeds via clustering-resampling; theoretical analysis of pseudo-seed impact on contrastive learning.
2024.contribution: PSQE plug-and-play module improves baseline precision and coverage balance, validated with theoretical guarantees.
2024.bp: Different databases describe the same real-world entities (people, companies, locations) using different schemas and modalities (text, images, structured fields). Aligning equivalent entities across sources enables merged knowledge bases, better NLP pipelines, and LLM-grounded retrieval. Seed pairs (known alignments) normally enable alignment, but collecting them is expensive.
2024.wh: Unsupervised alignment uses pseudo-seeds (guessed equivalences) from multimodal similarity. But modalities have different coverage: text may be rich for products, images for people. Pseudo-seeds accumulate in high-density regions (popular entities), leaving sparse-graph regions (niche entities) underrepresented. Contrastive learning then overfits to dense regions, ignoring sparse ones.
2024.ap: PSQE starts with coarse pseudo-seeds from multimodal similarity matching. Clustering groups entities by similarity, revealing sparse vs. dense regions. Resampling upweights pseudo-seeds in sparse regions, balancing coverage. The module sits as a preprocessing layer before any contrastive MMEA model.
2024.ww: Theoretical analysis shows pseudo-seeds affect both attraction (pulling matched pairs closer) and repulsion (pushing non-matches apart) terms in contrastive loss. Imbalanced coverage causes models to optimize only for dense-region repulsion (cheap, high gradient), neglecting sparse-region attraction. Resampling fixes gradient flow, letting the model learn uniformly.
2024.po: PSQE is a drop-in module for existing contrastive MMEA methods, improving baseline precision and enabling models to align sparse entities that were previously invisible. Knowledge-base merges become more complete, benefiting downstream NLP, retrieval-augmented generation, and LLM applications.

2025.problem: Deepfake detection methods generalize poorly; they rely on isolated spatial, temporal, or spectral cues without joint reasoning.
2025.approach: Lightweight spatial-spectral-temporal GNN that represents videos as structured graphs with learnable spectral filters.
2025.contribution: SSTGNN achieves superior cross-domain detection with 42× fewer parameters than state-of-the-art models.
2025.bp: AI-generated and manipulated videos are proliferating—deepfakes of politicians, revenge deepfakes, synthetic media. Detection is a cat-and-mouse game: the generator improves, detection must follow. Systems need fast, lightweight models deployable on phones and edges, and must generalize to new manipulation types unseen during training.
2025.wh: Separate spatial (inconsistent face geometry), temporal (unnatural eye blinks), and spectral (compression artifacts) detectors miss *interactions*. A video might pass all three individually but combine artifacts that only surface when analyzed jointly. Heavy CNNs work on known manipulations but fail on new ones. Edge deployment needs tiny models.
2025.ap: SSTGNN represents each video as a graph: nodes are spatial regions or frames, edges encode consistency (spatial adjacency, temporal continuity, or spectral correlation). A GNN with learnable spectral filters reasons over this graph, jointly weighing spatial inconsistencies, temporal artifacts, and spectral distortions. The graph structure forces joint reasoning.
2025.ww: Graph representations are sparse and lightweight compared to dense CNN feature maps. Spectral filters (learned Fourier bases) capture subtle frequency-domain manipulations (compression, generation artifacts). Spatial-temporal differential modeling (edge weights reflecting frame-to-frame changes) highlights unnatural transitions. Joint reasoning via message-passing catches correlations invisible to separate detectors.
2025.po: SSTGNN detects deepfakes with superior in-domain and cross-domain accuracy, using 42× fewer parameters than prior methods—deployable on mobile devices. Generalization improves: models trained on one manipulation type detect others better, addressing the cat-and-mouse arms race.
